paraphrase: Tsongkhapa, explaining the Saṃdhinirmocana's three natures, rejects the reading that the thoroughly established nature is an ultimate empty only of other things and not empty of itself: in the sūtra's own system the thoroughly established is the other-powered nature's emptiness of the imputational, and in the Madhyamaka nothing whatsoever, the ultimate included, is established by its own nature.
speaker: Tsongkhapa

paraphrase: Because the scriptures themselves differ — some to be taken literally, others requiring interpretation — which is definitive cannot be settled by citing scripture alone (else endless regress); it must be established by stainless reasoning, following the great charioteers Nāgārjuna and Asaṅga.

The Svātantrika hold that phenomena are posited by appearing to a non-defective awareness together with existing by their own character conventionally; the Prāsaṅgika hold that phenomena are posited only by the force of conceptual designation, with no existence from their own side even conventionally — this is the subtle difference in the object of negation.
The ultimate truth is the mere absence of inherent existence — a non-affirming negation — and emptiness itself is empty; there is no phenomenon, the ultimate included, that is ultimately established.
speaker: Tsongkhapa
notes: Doctrine well attested across Tsongkhapa's works; assignment to this section of the Essence of Eloquence is moderate confidence.
